bill.title: A joint resolution terminating the national emergency declared to impose global tariffs.
subjects: Presidents and presidential powers, Vice Presidents

industries.rationale: Manufacturers that import components or materials would see input costs change if the tariffs are removed.
Retailers and consumer goods companies that import finished products would face different cost structures depending on whether the tariffs remain.
Agricultural exporters and importers are directly affected by tariff policy and potential retaliatory measures from trading partners.
Technology companies that import hardware, semiconductors, or components face cost changes tied to tariff levels.
Shipping, logistics, and freight companies handle import volumes that shift with tariff policy changes.

bill.plainSummary: This joint resolution would end the national emergency that President Trump declared on April 2, 2025, which authorized a 10% tariff on most goods imported into the United States and higher tariffs on certain trading partners. Terminating the emergency would remove the legal basis for those tariffs. The resolution is a legislative tool for Congress to check executive emergency powers related to trade policy.

plain.whoItTouches: Anyone who buys imported goods, and people who make goods here.

bill.title: A joint resolution terminating the national emergency declared to impose duties on articles imported from Brazil.
subjects: Presidents and presidential powers, Vice Presidents

industries.rationale: Manufacturers importing Brazilian goods or components would see tariff costs change if the emergency and its 40% duty are terminated.
Retailers and consumer-goods companies importing products from Brazil would face different import costs depending on whether the tariff remains.
Agricultural importers bringing in Brazilian food products would be affected by the removal or continuation of the 40% tariff.
Importers of Brazilian metals and minerals face tariff exposure, though precious metals were already exempted from the additional duty.

bill.plainSummary: This resolution would end the national emergency that President Trump declared on July 30, 2025, which allowed the imposition of an additional 40% tariff on most goods imported from Brazil. Ending the emergency would remove the legal basis for those extra tariffs. Certain products—including aircraft parts, wood pulp, precious metals, energy products, and fertilizers—were already exempt from the additional tariff.

bill.title: Expedited Access to Biosimilars Act
bill.latestActionText: Placed on Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders. Calendar No. 520.
subjects: Drug safety, medical device, and laboratory regulation

industries.rationale: The bill directly addresses the regulatory approval process for biosimilar drugs, which would affect pharmaceutical and biotech manufacturers' market access and competitive landscape.
Faster biosimilar approval could reduce drug costs that health insurers cover, affecting their reimbursement obligations and formulary decisions.
Changes to biosimilar availability may affect which medications hospitals and physician groups can prescribe and the costs they incur for specialty drugs.

bill.plainSummary: This bill would create a faster approval pathway for biosimilar drugs—lower-cost alternatives to expensive biologic medications. The source material provides only the title and subject terms, which indicate the bill addresses drug regulation and licensing but does not specify what procedural or regulatory changes would be made. Without bill text or a summary, the exact mechanisms for expediting biosimilar access cannot be described.

bill.title: Laken Riley Act

industries.rationale: The bill directly imposes new detention mandates on DHS and creates liability exposure for federal agencies, while authorizing state governments to bring suit over immigration enforcement.

The bill creates new grounds for state litigation against the federal government and expands detention requirements, generating demand for legal services in immigration and intergovernmental litigation.

bill.plainSummary: This bill requires the Department of Homeland Security to detain certain non-citizens who are in the country unlawfully and have been arrested for or charged with crimes including burglary, theft, assault on law enforcement, or offenses causing death or serious injury. It also allows state governments to sue the federal government if immigration enforcement decisions or failures—such as releasing detainees, not conducting required asylum interviews, or violating parole limitations—cause harm to the state or its residents, including financial harm exceeding $100.

disclaimer: This tool places two public records next to each other: who donated to a member of Congress, and what that member legislated on. Any overlap you see is a correlation, not causation. It is not evidence of a quid pro quo, of influence, or of wrongdoing. Legislators routinely receive support from industries in their district for the same reason they legislate on them: those industries are there.
